opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the next big improvements will come less from brute-force scaling and more from a few directions.

The first is **data**. We've learned that caption quality matters enormously. Early models trained on noisy alt-text, and a lot of recent gains came from recaptioning datasets with richer, more accurate descriptions. I think there's still a lot of headroom in curating data more carefully: knowing what's in your training set, balancing it, and filtering for aesthetic and technical quality without losing diversity.

The second is **controllability**. Generating a beautiful image from a text prompt is close to solved for many use cases. But people doing real creative work don't just want a nice picture. They want *their* picture. They want to say "move that object a little to the left," "keep this character consistent across ten images," or "change the lighting but nothing else." Text is a pretty lossy interface for that. So I expect a lot of progress in editing, in conditioning on reference images, layouts, and sketches, and in multi-turn, conversational refinement where the model keeps track of what you've already established.

The third is **tighter integration with language and reasoning**. As image generation moves into the same models that understand language and other modalities, rather than a separate diffusion model bolted onto a text encoder, you get much better prompt following. Counting, spatial relationships, text rendering, and compositional prompts all improve because the model actually understands the request rather than pattern-matching on keywords.

Finally, I think **evaluation** is an underappreciated bottleneck. Our metrics, like FID and CLIP scores, don't capture what people actually care about. Human preference studies are expensive and noisy. Better ways to measure progress, especially for things like faithfulness, consistency, and usefulness in a real workflow, will help the whole field move faster, because right now it's hard to know whether a change is a real improvement.

So my short answer is better data, better control, deeper multimodal understanding, and better ways to measure all of it. The models are already impressive. The next step is making them useful collaborators rather than slot machines you pull until you get something you like.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the next big jumps won't come primarily from making the generative models themselves bigger. We've gotten to a point where, if you look at raw image quality, the samples are already really good. The models have learned a lot about how the world looks. So the frontier is shifting away from "can it make a pretty picture" toward a few other things.

The first is control and intent. Right now the dominant interface is a text prompt, and text is a pretty lossy way to describe an image. If you're an artist or a designer, you have a very specific thing in your head, and getting the model to produce that exact thing is still a lot of trial and error. So I think a lot of the improvement is going to come from richer conditioning: spatial controls, reference images, being able to say "keep this, change that," iterative editing that actually respects what was there before. Essentially moving from a slot machine to a tool.

The second is data and understanding. A lot of the failure modes people point to, hands, text rendering, compositional reasoning like "the cup is on the left of the book," are really about the model's understanding of the world, not its rendering ability. Better paired data, better captions, and borrowing more from the language and vision-language side will help there. I think we'll see tighter integration between understanding and generation, where the same system can reason about an image and then produce it.

Third, there's an efficiency story. Diffusion models have been expensive at inference time, and there's been a lot of work on distillation and fewer sampling steps. As that gets cheaper and faster, you unlock interactive use cases, real-time feedback loops, which in turn changes how people work with these models. Speed is a feature; it changes the creative process.

And then finally I'd say video and 3D are going to feed back into images. Once you train models that understand temporal consistency and geometry, you get a much better prior for single images too. So I expect the lines between those modalities to blur, and image generation to benefit from that.

If I had to bet, I'd say the headline improvements people notice over the next couple of years will feel less like "wow, it's more photorealistic" and more like "wow, it did exactly what I asked."

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the next major improvements will come from giving people more control over the generation process. Getting a beautiful image from a text prompt is impressive, but it’s different from getting the specific image you had in mind. You might like almost everything about a result and want to change just one thing, while keeping everything else consistent. That’s still a challenging problem.

So I’d expect progress in models that can take more kinds of input—a reference image, a sketch, or a sequence of edits—and make that interaction more predictable. There’s also room to improve their understanding of how objects relate to one another and how a scene fits together. To me, the exciting direction is making generation an iterative process where you can refine an idea, rather than repeatedly asking for a new image and hoping it matches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the next improvements will come from getting the models to understand more of what’s in an image and how those things relate to each other. We’ve made tremendous progress in generating images that look compelling at first glance. But if you ask for a very specific arrangement of objects, or several interacting constraints, you can still see gaps between what you asked for and what the model produces.

So one direction is better compositional understanding and control. Another is consistency: can you keep the same character or object while changing the viewpoint, the lighting, or the scene? That becomes especially important as you move toward video.

And I think the interaction will matter, too. Rather than having to get everything right in one prompt, you should be able to refine an image, make a local change, and preserve the parts you already like. That makes these models much more useful as creative tools.
